blocks.robotComment: "AI" gets used for everything from a chatbot to a killer robot in a movie — let's actually sort it out. 🤖
blocks.body: "AI" (artificial intelligence) is a broad umbrella term for software that performs tasks which normally require human intelligence — recognizing an image, answering a question, translating a sentence. It's not one specific technology; it's a whole category, the same way "vehicle" covers everything from a bicycle to a jet.

highlights.text: a broad umbrella term

blocks.body: Machine learning (ML) is a subset of AI: instead of a programmer writing exact rules for every situation, an ML system learns patterns directly from examples. Show it thousands of labeled photos of cats and dogs, and it gradually learns to tell them apart on its own — nobody hand-wrote a rule for "pointy ears usually mean cat."

highlights.text: Machine learning (ML) is a subset of AI

blocks.body: Deep learning is a subset of machine learning that uses neural networks — layered structures loosely inspired by neurons in a brain — with many layers stacked on top of each other. Almost every AI tool that's made headlines recently (chatbots, image generators, voice assistants) is built on deep learning specifically, not just "AI" in general.

highlights.text: Deep learning is a subset of machine learning

blocks.robotComment: This one distinction alone clears up most AI headlines once you have it. 📰
blocks.body: So the relationship nests like Russian dolls: AI is the biggest category, machine learning is one way of building AI, and deep learning is one particular kind of machine learning. A large language model like the ones behind modern chatbots is a deep learning system — meaning it's AI, and it's ML, but not every AI system is a deep learning system.

highlights.text: AI is the biggest category, machine learning is one way of building AI, and deep learning is one particular kind of machine learning

blocks.question: Which of these correctly describes how the three terms relate?
options: AI is the broadest category; machine learning is one way to build AI; deep learning is one kind of machine learning
Deep learning is the broadest category that contains AI and machine learning
AI, machine learning, and deep learning are three unrelated, separate fields
Machine learning is a newer replacement for AI — they mean the same thing today
blocks.explanation: They nest inside each other: AI is the umbrella, machine learning is one approach to building AI, and deep learning is one specific kind of machine learning.

blocks.sentence: A system that learns patterns from labeled examples instead of following hand-written rules is using ___.
options: machine learning
a search engine
a spreadsheet
blocks.explanation: Learning patterns from examples rather than explicit rules is the defining idea behind machine learning.

blocks.statement: Every AI system is a deep learning system.
blocks.explanation: Deep learning is only one kind of machine learning, which is only one way of building AI — plenty of AI (and even plenty of machine learning) doesn't use deep learning at all.

blocks.robotComment: It can feel like it's thinking. It's actually doing something much more mechanical underneath. ⚙️
blocks.body: At its core, a modern AI model is a pattern-matching system. During training, it's shown an enormous number of examples — text, images, whatever the task needs — and it adjusts millions or billions of internal numbers (called parameters) until its outputs start matching the patterns in that data.

highlights.text: a pattern-matching system

blocks.body: That's genuinely different from how a human learns a topic. A person builds an internal model of *why* something is true and can reason about situations they've never seen before. A trained AI model instead predicts what's statistically likely to come next, based on everything similar it saw during training — it doesn't have beliefs, intentions, or a real understanding of the world behind that prediction.

highlights.text: predicts what's statistically likely to come next

blocks.body: This is exactly why AI models sometimes confidently state something false — a behavior often called "hallucination." The model isn't lying on purpose; it's producing the most statistically plausible-sounding continuation, and plausible-sounding isn't the same thing as true. Nothing inside the system is actually checking the claim against reality.

highlights.text: hallucination

blocks.code:
What it feels like:  "The AI understood my question and thought about it."
What is actually happening:  The model converts your text into numbers,
  then predicts the most statistically likely next chunk of text,
  one piece at a time, based on patterns learned from training data.
blocks.caption: Same output, very different mechanism underneath — worth keeping straight.

blocks.question: Why do AI models sometimes state false things confidently ("hallucinate")?
options: They're producing the most statistically plausible-sounding output, which isn't the same as checking whether it's actually true
They are deliberately lying to the user
It only happens when the AI's internet connection is slow
It happens because the model is bored with the question
blocks.explanation: A model optimizes for plausible-sounding output based on patterns, with nothing built in that verifies the claim against reality.

blocks.sentence: When an AI model states something false while sounding completely confident, this is commonly called ___.
options: hallucination
debugging
compiling
blocks.explanation: That specific failure mode — confident, fluent, but factually wrong — has its own name: hallucination.

blocks.statement: An AI model predicting text is fundamentally doing the same thing as a human reasoning about why something is true.
blocks.explanation: A model predicts statistically likely continuations from patterns; it doesn't build the kind of causal, reasoned understanding a person does.

blocks.robotComment: No, none of today's AI is secretly plotting anything — it can't even want to. 😄
blocks.body: Every AI system in real use today is narrow AI: it's built and trained for a specific kind of task — writing text, generating images, recommending videos, detecting spam — and it doesn't generalize far beyond that. A model that's excellent at writing essays has no built-in ability to drive a car or plan a vacation; it would need to be an entirely different system for that.

highlights.text: narrow AI

blocks.body: Artificial general intelligence (AGI) is the hypothetical idea of a single AI system with human-level, flexible intelligence across essentially any task — able to learn a brand-new skill the way a person can, not just the one narrow thing it was trained on. AGI does not exist yet. It's an active research goal and a serious topic of debate, not a shipped product.

highlights.text: Artificial general intelligence (AGI)
does not exist yet

blocks.body: This matters because movies and headlines often blur the two together, which makes today's narrow tools sound far more capable — or far scarier — than they actually are. A chatbot that writes a great email is not a step away from general reasoning about the world; it's a highly capable narrow system doing one specific kind of pattern prediction very well.

highlights.text: movies and headlines often blur the two together

blocks.question: What best describes the AI tools in real, everyday use today?
options: Narrow AI — built and trained for a specific kind of task, without general intelligence
Artificial general intelligence (AGI), already fully achieved
Systems that are conscious and have their own goals
None of today's software actually counts as AI
blocks.explanation: Every deployed AI system today is narrow — good at a specific task, without human-like general intelligence across arbitrary tasks.

blocks.sentence: A hypothetical AI system with human-level, flexible intelligence across essentially any task is called ___.
options: artificial general intelligence (AGI)
a search engine
a spreadsheet macro
blocks.explanation: AGI is the term for that hypothetical, much broader kind of intelligence — and it hasn't been built yet.

blocks.statement: A chatbot that's very good at writing text also has a general ability to reason about any topic the way a person does.
blocks.explanation: Being highly capable at one kind of task (like writing) doesn't mean a system has general intelligence across unrelated tasks — that's exactly the narrow-vs-general distinction.

options: Predicting statistically likely output based on patterns learned from training data

Genuinely understanding and reasoning the way a human does

questions.statement: AI "hallucination" means the model is deliberately lying to the user.

questions.sentence: A confidently stated but false AI output is commonly called ___.
options: a hallucination

blocks.robotComment: No, it didn't read every book ever written personally — but it got shown an awful lot of pages. 📚
blocks.body: Training data is the huge collection of examples an AI model learns from before anyone ever gets to use it. For a model that works with text, that's an enormous amount of written material; for an image model, it might be millions of labeled photos; for a speech model, huge amounts of recorded audio. Whatever the task, training data is the raw material the model's patterns get built from.

highlights.text: Training data is the huge collection of examples an AI model learns from before anyone ever gets to use it

blocks.body: The word "huge" is doing real work here. Modern models are typically trained on datasets far too large for any one person to read in a lifetime — not a few hundred examples, but collections that would take centuries to read end to end. That scale is exactly what lets a model pick up patterns that are too subtle or too spread out for a small dataset to reveal.

highlights.text: collections that would take centuries to read end to end

blocks.body: It's easy to picture training data as a single tidy library, but in practice it's usually assembled from many different sources and formats, then cleaned up and organized before training even starts. The quality and variety of that data matters just as much as the sheer amount of it — a point this level comes back to shortly.

highlights.text: assembled from many different sources and formats

blocks.question: What is "training data," in plain terms?
options: The huge collection of examples an AI model learns from before it is ever used
A small handful of test questions given to the model after release
The instructions a programmer types to control the model in real time
A backup copy of the model itself
blocks.explanation: Training data is the large body of examples — text, images, audio, whatever fits the task — that the model learns patterns from during training.

blocks.sentence: The large collection of examples an AI model learns patterns from before it is ever used is called ___.
options: training data
a user manual
a search index
blocks.explanation: Training data is the raw material a model is shown during training so it can learn patterns from it.

blocks.statement: Modern AI models are typically trained on datasets small enough for one person to read in an afternoon.
blocks.explanation: It's the opposite — modern training datasets are typically far too large for any one person to read in a lifetime, which is part of why the patterns they contain can be so detailed.

blocks.robotComment: Billions of tiny dials, not one big brain switch. 🎛️
blocks.body: A "parameter" (also called a "weight") is just a number stored inside the model that controls how strongly one piece of information influences another. A model doesn't have beliefs or rules written out in sentences — it has a huge number of these adjustable numbers, and its entire behavior comes from their specific values.

highlights.text: A "parameter" (also called a "weight") is just a number stored inside the model that controls how strongly one piece of information influences another

blocks.body: Before training starts, these numbers are typically set to something close to random — the model genuinely knows nothing yet. Training is the process of gradually adjusting every one of those numbers, a tiny bit at a time, so the model's outputs get closer to what the training data suggests they should be.

highlights.text: Training is the process of gradually adjusting every one of those numbers

blocks.body: "Millions or billions of parameters" isn't a marketing exaggeration — it's a literal count of these adjustable numbers. More parameters generally means the model has more capacity to represent complicated patterns, though (as this level covers later) more isn't automatically better in every way.

highlights.text: it's a literal count of these adjustable numbers

blocks.code:
Before training:  parameter #4,829,301 = 0.0021  (close to random)
After training:   parameter #4,829,301 = -0.7734 (tuned by the data)

...repeated across every one of billions of parameters.
blocks.caption: Training doesn't rewrite the model — it retunes numbers like this one, over and over.

blocks.question: What is a "parameter" (or "weight") inside an AI model?
options: An adjustable number that controls how strongly one piece of information influences another
A line of written instructions the model follows like a recipe
A setting the end user changes in an app menu
A separate small program running alongside the main model
blocks.explanation: Parameters are the adjustable internal numbers whose specific values, after training, determine how the model behaves.

blocks.sentence: The process of gradually adjusting a model's parameters based on training data is called ___.
options: training
debugging
formatting
blocks.explanation: Training is exactly that gradual adjustment process — nudging the numbers so outputs better match the patterns in the data.

blocks.statement: A model's parameters are usually close to random before training begins.
blocks.explanation: That's right — before training, the numbers typically start out close to random, and training is what shapes them into something useful.

blocks.robotComment: Think of it as: study for the exam once, then take the exam over and over without opening the textbook again. 📖
blocks.body: Training and inference are two separate phases, and it's easy to blur them together. Training is the (often long, expensive) process of adjusting a model's parameters using training data. Inference is what happens every single time you actually use the finished model afterward — you give it an input, and it produces an output using the parameters that training already locked in.

highlights.text: Training and inference are two separate phases

blocks.body: During training, the model's parameters are actively changing. During inference, they're fixed — using the model doesn't adjust its underlying numbers at all. Asking a trained model a question is much more like running a finished calculation than it is like teaching the model something new in that moment.

highlights.text: During inference, they're fixed

blocks.body: This split also explains a cost difference people often don't expect: training a large model can take a long time on powerful hardware and can be genuinely expensive, while a single inference (one response to one question) is comparatively quick and cheap — even though it's the part users actually see.

highlights.text: training a large model can take a long time on powerful hardware and can be genuinely expensive

blocks.question: What is "inference," as distinct from training?
options: Using the already-trained model to produce an output from a new input, without changing its parameters
The process of first setting all the parameters to random values
A synonym for training — they mean the same thing
Deleting a model that is no longer needed
blocks.explanation: Inference is using the finished, already-trained model to respond to a new input — the parameters stay fixed during this step.

blocks.sentence: Every time you actually use a finished AI model to get a response, that single use is called ___.
options: inference
training
compiling
blocks.explanation: Inference is the term for a single use of an already-trained model to produce an output.

blocks.statement: A model's parameters keep changing every time someone uses it to answer a question.
blocks.explanation: Parameters are fixed during inference — using a trained model doesn't change its underlying numbers. Only training adjusts them.

questions.question: What is training data, in plain terms?
options: The huge collection of examples a model learns from before it is ever used
A short manual users read before using an app
A single test question given to the model after release
A backup file created after training finishes

questions.statement: Modern AI models are usually trained on datasets small enough for one person to read in a single sitting.

questions.sentence: A number inside a model that controls how strongly one piece of information influences another is called a ___.
options: parameter
a hyperlink
a font

questions.question: Before training begins, what are a model's parameters typically like?
options: Close to random values
Already perfectly tuned
Written out as plain-English rules
Copied directly from another finished model

questions.statement: A model's parameters keep changing every time someone asks it a question.

questions.sentence: The process of gradually adjusting a model's parameters using training data is called ___.
options: training
rendering
compiling

questions.question: What is inference?
options: Using an already-trained model to produce an output from a new input
The initial random setup of parameters
A synonym for training data
Permanently deleting a model

questions.statement: A model's entire behavior comes from the specific values of its many adjustable parameters.

questions.sentence: A single use of an already-trained model to answer one input is called one ___.
options: inference
dataset
parameter

questions.question: Which best describes the cost difference between training and inference?
options: Training a large model can take a long time and be expensive; a single inference is comparatively quick and cheap
Training is instant and free; inference is what actually costs money
They always cost exactly the same amount
Neither training nor inference has any real-world cost

chapters.title: What More Data & Compute Actually Buys You

lessons.title: Diminishing Returns: Why Bigger Isn't Always Better

blocks.robotComment: More data usually helps. It's not a free lunch, though. 🍽️
blocks.body: More training data and more computing power ("compute") generally make a model better — more examples to learn patterns from, and more processing capacity to actually learn from them. But this doesn't scale forever in a straight line: each additional chunk of data or compute tends to buy a smaller improvement than the chunk before it, a pattern called diminishing returns.

highlights.text: diminishing returns

blocks.body: Diminishing returns don't mean more data stops helping completely — they mean the improvement curve flattens out. Going from a tiny dataset to a medium one can produce a huge jump in quality; going from an already-enormous dataset to an even bigger one tends to produce a smaller, more incremental gain for the extra cost involved.

highlights.text: the improvement curve flattens out

blocks.body: And more data and compute have real costs, not just theoretical ones: training runs take real time on real hardware, that hardware costs real money to buy and run, and running large amounts of computing hardware uses real electricity — which has a real environmental footprint. None of that is a reason for panic, but it's a genuine trade-off, not a free resource.

highlights.text: a genuine trade-off, not a free resource

blocks.question: What does "diminishing returns" mean when it comes to training data and compute?
options: Each additional chunk of data or compute tends to produce a smaller improvement than the chunk before it
Adding more data always makes a model worse
After a certain point, adding data has zero cost at all
The first small dataset always produces the biggest possible model
blocks.explanation: Diminishing returns describes an improvement curve that flattens out — more still generally helps, but each additional amount buys less than the last.

blocks.sentence: The pattern where each additional chunk of training data or compute buys a smaller improvement than the last is called ___.
options: diminishing returns
a hallucination
inference
blocks.explanation: Diminishing returns is the standard term for an improvement curve that flattens out as more of something is added.

blocks.statement: Training large AI models has real costs in time, money, and electricity use.
blocks.explanation: Training runs require real computing time, real hardware costs, and real electricity — these are genuine, factual costs, not exaggeration.

lessons.title: Narrow Data In, Narrow Results Out

blocks.robotComment: A model can only reflect what it was actually shown — it can't invent knowledge from nowhere. 🪞
blocks.body: A model's outputs are shaped entirely by its training data. If that data is narrow — say, text from only one topic, one style, or one narrow slice of the world — the model tends to perform well only on that narrow slice and struggle or produce skewed results outside it. It never saw anything else to learn from.

highlights.text: A model's outputs are shaped entirely by its training data

blocks.body: The same idea applies to flawed or unrepresentative data, not just narrow data. If a dataset contains factual errors, skewed viewpoints, or systematically underrepresents certain groups or situations, the model tends to absorb those same issues into its patterns and reproduce them in its outputs — without knowing it's doing anything wrong.

highlights.text: the model tends to absorb those same issues into its patterns and reproduce them in its outputs

blocks.body: This is why the people building a model care so much about what goes into training, not just how much of it there is. A model trained on a huge pile of low-quality or narrow data isn't automatically better than one trained on a smaller, more carefully chosen dataset — quality and coverage matter alongside sheer scale.

highlights.text: isn't automatically better than one trained on a smaller, more carefully chosen dataset

blocks.question: What tends to happen when a model is trained on narrow or flawed data?
options: The model tends to reflect that same narrowness or those same flaws in its outputs
The model automatically corrects the flaws on its own
The size of the dataset stops mattering entirely
The model refuses to produce any output at all
blocks.explanation: A model has no way to know what it wasn't shown — narrow or flawed training data tends to produce narrow or flawed outputs.

blocks.sentence: A model's outputs are shaped by its training data, so data that is narrow or flawed tends to produce results that are similarly ___.
options: narrow or flawed
more accurate
completely random
blocks.explanation: A model can only reflect patterns it was actually shown — problems in the training data tend to show up in the outputs too.

blocks.statement: A bigger training dataset is always better than a smaller one, regardless of quality.
blocks.explanation: Scale alone isn't enough — a smaller, higher-quality and more representative dataset can outperform a huge but narrow or flawed one.

blocks.robotComment: It's not eavesdropping on your last conversation and quietly updating itself — that's not how this works. 🧊
blocks.body: Once training finishes, a model's parameters are typically frozen: they stay exactly as training left them while people actually use the model. This surprises a lot of people, because it means most consumer AI tools do not learn from your individual conversations in real time the way a person would after talking to you.

highlights.text: a model's parameters are typically frozen

blocks.body: Within a single conversation, a model can appear to "remember" what you said earlier — but that's because your earlier messages are being fed back in as part of the current input (more on this in Level 4), not because its underlying parameters changed. Once that conversation ends, none of it has altered the model itself.

highlights.text: your earlier messages are being fed back in as part of the current input

blocks.body: Updating a model's actual parameters again generally requires a separate, deliberate retraining or fine-tuning process, run by whoever built it — not something that happens automatically as a side effect of ordinary conversations. It's a meaningful distinction: a frozen model behaves consistently between updates, for better or worse.

highlights.text: a separate, deliberate retraining or fine-tuning process

blocks.question: Do most consumer AI chatbots permanently learn from your individual conversations with them in real time?
options: No — their parameters are typically frozen after training and stay fixed while people use them
Yes — every message you send instantly and permanently changes the model
Yes, but only for the first conversation you ever have with it
No AI model has ever been trained on conversation data of any kind
blocks.explanation: A model's parameters are frozen after training. Ordinary use (inference) doesn't change them — updating them requires a separate retraining process.

blocks.sentence: After training ends, a model's parameters are typically ___, meaning ordinary use does not change them.
options: frozen
deleted
randomized
blocks.explanation: Frozen means the parameters stay fixed at whatever training left them at — using the model doesn't alter them.

blocks.statement: A model appearing to remember earlier messages in the same conversation means its underlying parameters have changed.
blocks.explanation: That apparent memory comes from earlier messages being fed back in as part of the current input, not from any change to the model's actual parameters.
